column5: The storefront ships Figtree as its sans typeface while the documented and redesign target is Plus Jakarta Sans which is not loaded anywhere
column6: CLAUDE.md is explicit in three places that the storefront sans is Plus Jakarta Sans at weights 400 to 800 loaded through next/font/google in src/config/fonts.ts - the tech stack table in section 2 - the redesign token block - and section 9 rule 13 which adds that Figtree remains ONLY as the --font-mono fallback face. The redesign notes list Figtree among the stale values that must not be reintroduced and section 6.7 makes font is Plus Jakarta Sans an explicit visual regression check. The shipped code does the opposite. A search of src and tailwind.config.ts for Plus Jakarta Sans returns nothing so the family is not loaded at all. src/styles/globals.css:304 defines --font-sans as Figtree with system fallbacks - tailwind.config.ts:20 maps sans to var(--font-sans) so every font-sans class resolves to Figtree - src/config/fonts.ts:7-14 exports fontSans as a plain descriptor naming the Figtree family - and src/pages/_document.tsx:16-27 pulls Figtree from Google Fonts through a stylesheet link whose comment calls it the site sans typeface. next/font is used only for the self-hosted Figtree that backs --font-mono at src/config/fonts.ts:16-17.
column10: Every page - the typeface is global.
column11: 1. Load any storefront page. 2. Inspect the computed font-family on body or any text node. 3. Compare against the redesign sandbox target and against CLAUDE.md section 2.
column12: Text renders in Plus Jakarta Sans loaded via next/font/google as the documentation and the redesign target require - with Figtree confined to the mono fallback.
column13: Every screen renders in Figtree because that is what --font-sans resolves to and Plus Jakarta Sans is never loaded.
column14: The entire reskin renders in the wrong typeface so every screen diverges from its redesign twin on letterforms - weights and vertical rhythm. It is invisible when reviewing screens one at a time which is why it survived the earlier sessions. The Google Fonts stylesheet is also render blocking and needs two extra preconnects which next/font/google would remove.
column15: Load Plus Jakarta Sans through next/font/google in src/config/fonts.ts at weights 400 to 800 and point --font-sans at it - then delete the Google Fonts link and the two preconnects from _document.tsx. Keep Figtree only as the --font-mono face. Verify at /design-system which section 6.7 names as the regression target.

column5: Direction sensitive spacing and alignment use physical Tailwind classes so the Arabic layout does not mirror
column6: CLAUDE.md section 6.5 requires logical properties - ms and me and ps and pe rather than ml and mr and pl and pr - so the Arabic right-to-left layout mirrors correctly. The codebase does the reverse. Across src the physical margin and padding classes appear 57 times in 32 files and text-left or text-right a further 23 times - against only 4 uses of the logical ms me ps pe forms and 9 of text-start or text-end. Tailwind does not mirror physical utilities automatically and no RTL plugin is installed - neither tailwind.config.ts nor package.json references one - so each of those roughly 80 declarations keeps its left or right meaning when the document direction flips to rtl. The direction attribute itself is applied correctly at src/pages/_app.tsx:58-61 so the page does switch to rtl - which is precisely what exposes the mismatch.
column10: Application language set to Arabic which forces right-to-left per the i18n configuration.
column11: 1. Switch the language to Arabic. 2. Open screens that use directional spacing such as the cart rows - the checkout summary and the product cards. 3. Compare the gaps and text alignment against the left-to-right rendering.
column12: Spacing and alignment mirror with the text so an Arabic layout is the mirror image of the English one.
column13: Roughly 80 spacing and alignment declarations keep their physical side so gaps land on the wrong side of elements and text alignment fights the paragraph direction.
column14: Arabic is a supported and shipped language and its layout is visibly broken wherever directional spacing is used. Because the direction attribute already flips correctly the text runs right-to-left while the spacing does not which reads worse than no RTL support at all.
column15: Convert the physical utilities to their logical equivalents - ml to ms and mr to me and pl to ps and pr to pe and text-left or text-right to text-start or text-end. Convert opportunistically per file as CLAUDE.md prescribes for this kind of debt rather than in one sweep - and add an eslint rule or a review check so new physical utilities are not introduced.

column5: Twenty two of the forty one icon-only buttons have no accessible name
column6: CLAUDE.md section 6.5 requires an aria-label on every icon-only control and pairs it with a tooltip. Scanning every tsx file for isIconOnly and checking an eight line window either side for aria-label or aria-labelledby finds 41 icon-only buttons of which 22 have no accessible name - spread across 13 files including src/components/Cards/ProductCard.tsx - ProductCardAddButton.tsx - Cart/AttachmentUploader.tsx - Cart/PromoCodeSection.tsx - Functional/GlobalSearchbar.tsx and Functional/ScrollToTopButton.tsx. The remaining 19 are labelled correctly so the convention is understood and applied inconsistently rather than unknown. A button whose only content is an icon exposes no text to assistive technology so each of these announces as button with no indication of what it does.
column10: Screen reader or any assistive technology on screens carrying icon-only controls - the product card wishlist and cart buttons are on every listing.
column11: 1. Open a product listing with a screen reader. 2. Move through the interactive elements on a product card. 3. Listen to how the wishlist and add-to-cart buttons are announced.
column12: Every icon-only control announces its purpose through an aria-label as the 19 correctly labelled instances already do.
column13: Twenty two controls announce only as a button with no name so their purpose is unavailable without sight of the icon.
column14: Core shopping actions including add to cart and add to wishlist are unusable by screen reader users on the most repeated component in the catalogue. It is also a straightforward WCAG 2.1 AA failure under name role value.
column15: Add an aria-label sourced from the existing translation keys to each unlabelled control and pair it with a Tooltip as section 6.5 requires. eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y is already active through eslint-config-next so tightening the relevant rule to error would prevent regressions.

column5: The application has no React error boundary and no custom error page so a render error blanks the whole page
column6: A repository wide search for ErrorBoundary and componentDidCatch across src returns no results so no error boundary exists anywhere in the tree. There is also no src/pages/_error.tsx and no src/pages/500.tsx. React unmounts the entire tree when a render throws and with no boundary to catch it the customer is left with a blank page and no route back - while a server side or client runtime error falls through to the default Next.js error screen which is unstyled and untranslated and carries none of the storefront chrome. The application does ship ui/ErrorState and uses it correctly for FAILED REQUESTS on many screens - this gap is specifically about thrown render errors which that component cannot catch. Standard practice is a boundary in _app.tsx plus boundaries around independently failing regions such as home sections and product detail blocks.
column10: Any component that throws during render - a malformed API payload reaching a component that indexes into it is the most likely trigger given the shape guards found elsewhere in this review.
column11: 1. Cause any component to throw during render - for example by returning a payload whose expected array field is absent to a component that maps over it. 2. Observe the page.
column12: The failing region is replaced by an error state with a recovery action while the rest of the page keeps working.
column13: The whole page unmounts to blank with no message and no way forward other than a manual reload.
column14: A single unhandled render error takes down the entire storefront page rather than one region. Combined with the absence of a styled 500 page every uncaught runtime failure presents to the customer as either a blank screen or an unbranded Next.js error page.
column15: Add an error boundary in _app.tsx that renders ui/ErrorState with a retry - add boundaries around independently failing regions - and add a styled and translated src/pages/_error.tsx and 500 page so runtime failures stay inside the storefront design.

column5: The html lang attribute is hard-coded to English in the document and is only corrected on the client after hydration
column6: src/pages/_document.tsx:5 renders Html with lang set to the literal string en and nothing in the document updates it. The correction happens only in the browser - src/pages/_app.tsx:59 and :62 call documentElement.setAttribute for lang and :58 and :61 do the same for dir once the language is known. Every server response therefore declares English regardless of the visitor language and the direction attribute is likewise absent from the initial HTML. Anything that consumes the response before hydration sees the wrong values - search engine crawlers - a screen reader beginning to read during load - and the first paint which renders left-to-right before flipping to rtl for Arabic. The client side handling itself is correct so this is specifically about the server rendered document.
column10: Arabic or Hindi visitor on a server rendered page - and any crawler or assistive technology reading the initial response.
column11: 1. Set the language to Arabic. 2. Request any page and read the raw HTML before JavaScript runs with view-source or curl. 3. Read the lang and dir attributes on the html element.
column12: The document declares the visitor language and direction in the server response.
column13: The server response always declares lang en and carries no dir so Arabic pages start as English left-to-right and flip after hydration.
column14: Screen readers may apply English pronunciation rules to Arabic and Hindi content read during load - search engines see every localised page as English which undermines localised indexing - and Arabic users see a brief left-to-right flash before the direction corrects.
column15: Read the language from the request in _document getInitialProps or from the locale cookie and set lang and dir on the Html element server side - keeping the existing _app effect as the client side update when the language changes without a reload.
